lesson.title: Undoing Multiplication: An Introduction to Factoring
lesson.summary: Factoring rewrites a polynomial as a product of simpler factors, reversing multiplication, and sets up the specific techniques covered throughout the rest of this unit.
lesson.body:
Factoring a polynomial means writing it as a product of two or more simpler polynomials, the factors, instead of a sum of terms. It is the reverse operation of everything you have been doing so far in this unit: multiplying polynomials takes factors and combines them into one expanded expression, while factoring takes an expanded expression and breaks it back into factors. Since a polynomial is built from terms, and factoring undoes multiplication, understanding what a polynomial is and how multiplication distributes across it is essential before factoring makes any sense.

Factoring matters because many algebra problems become far easier to solve once an expression is written as a product. If a product of factors equals zero, then at least one of those factors must itself be zero, a fact called the zero product property. This turns equations that look complicated in expanded form into simple ones once factored. For instance, once x^2 + 5x + 6 is known to equal (x + 2)(x + 3), the equation x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0 becomes (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, and the zero product property says either x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0, giving the two solutions x = -2 and x = -3 almost immediately. Factoring is also used constantly to simplify fractions containing polynomials and to identify the roots of an equation quickly.

The idea of factoring is easiest to see first with plain numbers. The number 6 can be factored as 2 times 3; both factors are simpler than 6 itself, and multiplying them back gives 6 again. Polynomials work the same way. Take x^2 + 5x + 6. To factor this trinomial, look for two numbers that multiply to give the constant term, 6, and add to give the coefficient of the middle term, 5. The numbers 2 and 3 satisfy both conditions: 2 times 3 is 6, and 2 plus 3 is 5. So the trinomial factors as (x + 2)(x + 3).

You always have a built in way to check factoring: multiply the factors back together and confirm you recover the original polynomial. Using FOIL on (x + 2)(x + 3) gives x^2 + 3x + 2x + 6, and combining like terms gives x^2 + 5x + 6, which matches the original expression exactly. Whenever you factor anything in this unit, this check, multiplying back out, is your safety net against errors.

Not every polynomial factors the same way, so the rest of this unit introduces several specific techniques: pulling out a greatest common factor, factoring trinomials by finding a matching pair of numbers, and recognizing special structures like a difference of squares or a perfect square trinomial, as well as factoring by grouping for polynomials with four terms. Each technique is a tool suited to a particular pattern, and part of becoming skilled at factoring is learning to recognize which tool a given polynomial calls for.

One more habit is worth building from the start: factoring completely. Sometimes a factor you find can itself be broken down further, and a polynomial is not considered fully factored until none of its remaining factors can be split any more. This unit will return to that idea repeatedly, since checking for a greatest common factor before applying any other technique, and then checking whether the resulting factors hide a further pattern, is what turns a partial factoring into a complete one.
